meta.source_text: Rahlfs-Hanhart, Septuaginta (the Nehemiah portion of Esdras B)

preamble.summary: In the Greek tradition, Nehemiah is not a separate book but part of Esdras B, numbered continuously with Ezra. The translation is close to the Hebrew throughout. The key translation choices concern the covenant-keeping formula at 1:5, the Torah-reading-with-interpretation passage at 8:8 that shaped later synagogue and church practice, and the great covenant-confession of chapter 9 that is one of the fullest recapitulations of salvation history in the Hebrew Bible.
preamble.notable_variants: The ho theos tou ouranou formula at 1:5 that links Ezra-Nehemiah to Revelation's 'God of heaven'; the methodological note at 8:8 on reading Scripture meporash ('with clear interpretation') that becomes the rabbinic and patristic model of public Scripture-reading; the divine attributes catalog at 9:17 that echoes Exodus 34:6 and reappears across Hellenistic Jewish prayer; and the exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites at 13:1 that Ruth narratively contests.
preamble.theological_legacy: Nehemiah 8:8 in its LXX form — reading with explanation (diesteilen) so the people understand — is one of the foundational texts for Jewish and Christian liturgical practice of public Scripture reading with homiletical exposition. The Acts 8 account of Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch ('do you understand what you are reading?') draws on this Nehemiah 8 model.

renderings.mt_reading: הָאֵל הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא שֹׁמֵר הַבְּרִית וָחֶסֶד
renderings.lxx_reading: ὁ θεὸς ὁ μέγας καὶ ὁ φοβερός φυλάσσων τὴν διαθήκην καὶ τὸ ἔλεος
renderings.mt_rendering: the great and awe-inspiring God who keeps covenant and faithful love
renderings.lxx_rendering: the God, the great and the fearful, who keeps the covenant and mercy
notes: The LXX's diathēkē ('covenant') and eleos ('mercy') are the fixed equivalents for Hebrew berit and chesed in Hellenistic Jewish discourse. The pairing 'covenant and mercy/steadfast love' is a formulaic phrase that recurs at Deuteronomy 7:9, 1 Kings 8:23, Daniel 9:4, Nehemiah 1:5 and 9:32 — a signature of deuteronomistic covenant theology.
Luke 1:72 ('to show mercy to our ancestors, to remember his holy covenant') uses the same LXX diathēkē-plus-eleos word-pair when Zechariah's Benedictus recalls God's covenant faithfulness.

renderings.mt_reading: וַיִּקְרְאוּ בַסֵּפֶר בְּתוֹרַת הָאֱלֹהִים מְפֹרָשׁ וְשׂוֹם שֶׂכֶל וַיָּבִינוּ בַּמִּקְרָא
renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἀνέγνωσαν ἐν βιβλίῳ νόμου τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐδίδασκεν Εσδρας καὶ διέστελλεν ἐν ἐπιστήμῃ κυρίου καὶ συνῆκεν ὁ λαὸς ἐν τῇ ἀναγνώσει
renderings.mt_rendering: They read from the scroll of the Law of God, translating and giving the meaning so that the people understood what was being read
renderings.lxx_rendering: And they read in the book of the Law of God, and Ezra taught and gave distinction in the knowledge of the Lord, and the people understood in the reading
notes: The Hebrew meforash ('distinctly, with explanation') is debated: some read it as evidence of targumic translation (Aramaic rendering of the Hebrew text for the post-exilic community), others as homiletical exposition. The LXX's diestellen en epistēmē ('gave distinction in knowledge') captures the exposition sense — Ezra is teaching with interpretive skill.

Acts 8:30–35 (Philip and the Ethiopian) reads almost as a narrative dramatization of Nehemiah 8:8: a teacher reads aloud, a student does not understand, the interpreter 'opens up' (Acts 8:35 diēnoixen) the Scripture and the hearer understands. The structural template is LXX-Nehemiah-8.
Nehemiah 8:8 is one of the primary OT texts for the theology of Scripture-reading as an interpretive practice that requires a community of teachers and learners.

renderings.mt_reading: אֱלוֹהַּ סְלִיחוֹת חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם אֶרֶךְ־אַפַּיִם וְרַב־חֶסֶד
renderings.lxx_reading: θεὸς ἐπιεικὴς καὶ ἐλεήμων μακρόθυμος καὶ πολυέλεος
renderings.mt_rendering: a God of forgiveness — gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and rich in faithful love
renderings.lxx_rendering: a God forbearing and merciful, patient and full of mercy
notes: Nehemiah 9:17 echoes the Exodus 34:6 divine-attributes formula — 'merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love' — which is the most theologically consequential self-description of YHWH in the Hebrew Bible. The LXX renders the formula with epieikēs, eleēmōn, makrothymos, polyeleos.

James 5:11 ('the Lord is polysplanchnos and oiktirmōn') and NT descriptions of God's forbearance (Rom 2:4, 2 Pet 3:9) draw on this extended LXX word-cluster. The same divine-attributes formula recurs across LXX Numbers 14:18, Psalms 86/85:15 and 103/102:8, Jonah 4:2, Joel 2:13, Nahum 1:3 — a steady LXX refrain.

The formula's specific language is rabbinic ('the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy') and patristic ('the mercy-name of God'). Both traditions work from the Hebrew original and its LXX translation as a fixed liturgical text.

renderings.mt_reading: אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָבוֹא עַמֹּנִי וּמֹאָבִי בִּקְהַל הָאֱלֹהִים
renderings.lxx_reading: οὐκ εἰσελεύσονται Αμμανῖται καὶ Μωαβῖται εἰς ἐκκλησίαν θεοῦ
renderings.mt_rendering: no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God
renderings.lxx_rendering: Ammonites and Moabites shall not enter into the assembly of God
notes: The LXX's ekklēsia theou ('assembly of God') is the exact phrase Paul uses for the Christian church (1 Cor 1:2, 11:22; Gal 1:13; 1 Tim 3:5, 15). The Pauline ekklēsia tou theou is the same Greek phrase that LXX Nehemiah uses for the qahal Elohim — the gathered covenant community of Israel.

The inclusion-of-Gentiles question in early Christianity presses against the LXX-Nehemiah principle. Ruth (a Moabite) and Naaman (a Syrian) become the NT's favored counter-texts: God has always accepted the foreigner in faith. The tension between LXX Nehemiah 13 and LXX Ruth is internal to the Greek Bible itself.
Acts 10 (Peter and Cornelius) and Galatians 3:28 ('there is neither Jew nor Greek') can be read as the NT's programmatic resolution of this tension.
